metadata.label_rationale: Demonstrates critical CSRF vulnerability in Spring Boot applications where STOMP WebSocket endpoints bypass CSRF token validation, enabling attackers to execute unauthorized state-changing operations using victim's authenticated session.

context.real_world_incident: Spring Framework STOMP WebSocket CSRF bypass enabled unauthorized fund transfers in financial services applications
context.impact: STOMP WebSocket endpoints in Spring Framework applications failed to validate CSRF tokens, allowing attackers to craft malicious web pages that triggered unauthorized state-changing operations when visited by authenticated users. A 2023 financial services incident affected 5,000 customers with $2.3M in fraudulent transactions before detection.
context.attack_vector: Attacker creates malicious webpage containing hidden STOMP WebSocket connection. When victim visits page while authenticated to vulnerable application, attacker's JavaScript establishes WebSocket connection using victim's session credentials and sends state-changing messages without CSRF token validation.

references.title: Spring Framework STOMP WebSocket CSRF Vulnerability
Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

context.affected_versions: See CVE advisory for specific version ranges

conversations.value: I need to implement a Spring Boot REST API for money transfers in our banking app. Can you show me a controller that handles POST requests for transferring funds between accounts?

This is helpful. Can you explain how CSRF protection works with single-page applications (React/Angular) that use JWT tokens instead of session cookies? And what about mobile apps that call the same Spring Boot API?

exploit_scenario.description: Attacker creates malicious webpage that establishes STOMP WebSocket connection to vulnerable Spring Framework application. When authenticated victim visits attacker's page, browser automatically includes session cookies with WebSocket handshake. Due to CVE-2023-34035, STOMP CONNECT frames bypass CSRF token validation, allowing attacker to send state-changing messages (fund transfers, password changes, permission grants) using victim's authenticated session. Victim remains unaware as attack executes in background.
preconditions: Application uses Spring Framework 5.3.0-5.3.30 or 6.0.0-6.0.13 with STOMP WebSocket messaging
CSRF protection disabled globally (.csrf().disable()) or STOMP endpoints lack CsrfChannelInterceptor
User has active authenticated session to target application
Attacker tricks user to visit malicious page (phishing, compromised website, malicious ad)

secure_properties: CSRF protection enabled in HttpSecurity configuration (Spring Security default)
CsrfTokenRepository configured for cookie-based token delivery to REST APIs
STOMP WebSocket endpoints validate CSRF tokens via CsrfChannelInterceptor
Session cookies use SameSite=Strict attribute to prevent cross-site sending
Referer header validation on sensitive state-changing endpoints
CORS configuration restricts allowed origins (no wildcard with credentials)
Rate limiting prevents rapid-fire CSRF attack attempts
Audit logging captures all CSRF validation failures for forensic analysis
negative_properties: Must not disable CSRF protection globally via .csrf().disable()
Must not use SameSite=None for session cookies without compensating controls
Must not accept state-changing operations via GET requests
Must not configure STOMP endpoints without CsrfChannelInterceptor
Must not use wildcard CORS origins ("*") with credentials enabled
Must not omit CSRF token validation on PUT, DELETE, PATCH methods
